issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Since the collision, Emmanuel, a 68-year-old widowed African American dancer, has measured time as before and after the afternoon his car was struck in an intersection by a speeding driver. He remembers the violent sideways force, the scream of metal, and the sense that his body had suddenly become something he could no longer command. What remains most vivid is not a clean sequence but flashes: the steering wheel jerking, a burst of sound, glass, a trapped feeling, then gaps. Even now he says he cannot tell himself a clear story of what happened from beginning to end. When he tries on purpose to go back over it, his mind catches on fragments and then goes blank, and the missing parts leave him feeling exposed to something he still does not fully understand.

In the weeks afterward, that broken quality of the memory became bound up with the conclusions he drew about himself and the world. Because he could not form a coherent account of what he had done, or failed to do, during the crash, Emmanuel had come to believe he could not trust himself to do the right thing in danger. The collision also changed how he thought about his body. As a dancer, he had spent decades relying on balance, timing, and physical control; now the fact that his body had been so suddenly overpowered felt like proof that it was unreliable. He also spoke bitterly about how the systems that should have protected him had not done so, returning to the conviction that people and institutions had failed him. Those beliefs did not sit as abstract opinions. They sharpened the memory into something more threatening: if he could not trust his own body, if he could not trust his judgment, if protection could not be counted on, then danger could arrive without warning and he would not be able to meet it.

That sense of ongoing vulnerability began to organize Emmanuel's days. In restaurants, rehearsal spaces, and waiting rooms, he felt unsafe unless he could sit with his back against a wall and see the whole room. At his dance studio, what had once been a familiar place became a setting he scanned constantly; if music started abruptly or a door slammed in the hall, he jolted and stayed on edge. Delays unsettled him in the same way. If a fellow performer was late or a ride took longer than expected, he quickly assumed something bad was happening. These reactions were fed by the same beliefs that had settled in after the crash: that his body might not respond properly, that he might misjudge what to do, that safety could not be assumed.

The memory problems also drove this vigilance. Because the collision existed for him as scattered pieces rather than a whole event, unexpected sounds and moments of uncertainty seemed to connect directly to those fragments without warning. A loud noise did not just startle him; it felt like the beginning of something terrible whose ending he could not fully remember. Not being able to deliberately retrieve the memory made him feel less prepared, as if the missing parts contained crucial information he needed in order to stay safe now. In that way, the gaps themselves kept him scanning for danger.

Over months, Emmanuel responded by steadily narrowing his life. He stopped going out unless he had to. He avoided seeing people he used to socialize with before the collision, in part because being with them pulled him toward questions about what had happened that he could not answer clearly, and in part because being out among people and noise left him feeling exposed. When therapy began, he found himself skirting anything that touched the crash too directly; after sessions in which it was discussed, he tried hard not to think about what had come up. These habits made sense to him. If he stayed home, kept away from old social circles, and pushed away therapy content, he was less likely to be confronted by the fragments he could not organize and less likely to feel that surge of danger.

But the avoidance tightened the problem. The less he went out, the more unfamiliar and risky the outside world felt. The less he tolerated hearing or speaking about the collision, the more incomplete and inaccessible the memory seemed, and the more he felt he had no reliable internal guide. His hypervigilance filled the space left by the life he had withdrawn from: sitting with his back to walls, watching doors, bracing at sounds, assuming the worst when anything ran late. At the studio, this has cost him work and belonging; he has cut back his presence there, and the community that once held him since his wife's death has become harder to reach.

By the time he sought help again, Emmanuel was living in a constricted routine organized around not being caught off guard. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he was losing not only work but the part of himself that had always felt most certain in motion. He is most afraid that the crash proved something permanent-that he cannot trust his body, his judgment, or the people meant to keep him safe. What he hopes, though cautiously, is that he might one day remember without coming apart and return to a room without needing to guard every exit.
